Every colour in the collection

426 colour slots across 40 puzzles, three ways: what upstream’s C computes, what this app draws on a light board, and what it draws on a dark one. Generated by scripts/build-palette.mjs — no hex is written by hand.

Where each column comes from

upstream — vendor/sgtpuzzles/<game>.c, compiled and asked. The colours are static inside each puzzle and reachable only through its game struct, so a harness links one puzzle against the collection’s core and calls thegame.colours() — the same call the midend makes at startup. The frontend stub is emcc.c’s, copied: 0.9F grey, then whatever the page says. Upstream’s page says nothing and neither does ours, so every puzzle in the collection is built on the same 0.9 grey. The hex is formatted by emcc.c’s own sprintf line, in the C, because the rounding is single precision and it matters: 255 * 0.9f rounds to exactly 229.5, which carries to #e6, where the same sum in double truncates to #e5.

light — the strings js_set_colour delivers, caught by booting the shipped wasm with a host that records and does nothing else. This is named[] in the renderer, before palette.ts runs.

dark — forDarkBoard(named, game), which is what the renderer swaps in.

The light board is upstream’s board

The first two columns are independent routes to the same fact — one compiles the C, the other runs the shipped wasm through this app’s own JavaScript — and they agree on all 426 slots. Nothing this port does changes a colour on a light board. The generator exits non-zero if that ever stops being true, so the claim is checked rather than made.

The three rules

Applied by forDarkBoard in this order. One distinction is behind them: a puzzle’s structure lives in its neutrals and wants to be the other way up on a dark surface; its meaning lives in its hues — Mines’ digits, Map’s regions, Tents’ grass — and inverting those would be a lie.

compress 26 slots
A grey whose being black or white is something the rules say. Kept the way up it started, only pulled into the dark board’s range. Black stays black. Listed per game in SEMANTIC, because the line is not quite where saturation puts it: Pearl’s two circles carry meaning and have no hue at all.
veil 198 slots
Anything with a hue at or above ACHROMATIC. Kept, with black laid over it in proportion to how much light it throws.
flip 194 slots
Every other grey: the board, the shading, the ink, the lines. Turned over into [FLOOR, CEILING].
derived 8 slots
Ahead of the other three, and the reason they do not reach these: the C defines the colour as a shade of its board. Those keep the contrast they had against the board, the other way round.

Which rule a slot takes is computed from its saturation for all but the 34 slots named in the two tables below. No colour on this page was chosen. Every dark value is the output of one of these rules, and the bevel correction adds none either — it exchanges two values a rule already produced.

Parameters

The numbers the rules are tuned by. All are in src/engine/palette.ts.

namevaluewhat it does
ACHROMATIC0.15Saturation at or above which a colour is carrying meaning, and is veiled rather than flipped. The single number that sorts 392 of the 426 slots into their rule.
FLOOR0.06The dark board's lightest black. A flip maps into [FLOOR, CEILING] rather than to 1 − l, so nothing lands on pure black or pure white.
CEILING0.82The dark board's darkest white, same reason.
VEIL0.35How much black is laid over a hue at its brightest. Upstream chose its hues against a white board; at full strength they are the loudest thing on a dark one.
SEMANTIC_BOARD0.26Where a board goes when it has to move out from under a black the rules keep — the games in SEMANTIC whose kept grey would otherwise be darker than the flipped board.
PAPER_BOARD0.49The same, for the two games whose white half is the board itself rather than something drawn on it.
NUDGES[-0.09, 0.09, -0.17, 0.17, -0.25, 0.25, -0.33, 0.33]Offsets tried, in order, when a veiled colour lands too close to something it has to be told apart from.

Corrections and exceptions

Laid over the three rules. The first two change a colour; the last three are decided where the shape is drawn, not in the palette, because the palette has one colour per slot and these need two.

SEMANTIC — 10 games
Slots whose being black or white is something the rules say. Compressed into the dark range the way up they started, rather than turned over.
pattern, flip, pearl, unruly, mosaic, singles, range, lightup, guess, blackbox
DERIVED — 4 games
Slots the C defines as a shade of the board — `ret[COL_X] = ret[COL_BACKGROUND] * k`. They keep the contrast upstream gave them against the board, the other way round, found by bisection.
blackbox, lightup, loopy, palisade
BEVEL — 10 games
Pairs that are a lit and a shaded edge of the same relief. The rules are about what a colour is; relief is about where the light comes from, so after the rules run the pair is swapped if the lit side did not come out lighter.
fifteen, sixteen, twiddle, mines, samegame, pegs, blackbox, inertia, flood, unruly
FIGURE — 1 game
Slots that are a picture drawn on the board rather than part of it — Undead's three monsters. On a dark board these are served their light values, and only where the call is a shape.
undead
RIM — 1 game
Where a fill and its outline are the same slot, and a table of colours by slot has only one colour to give. Dark boards only, and only where the two arrive equal.
pearl
BOARD_IS_PAPER — 2 games
The games whose white half is the board, so nothing is painted white on them. Their board is raised to PAPER_BOARD rather than SEMANTIC_BOARD when it has to move. Declared rather than computed: whether a slot is ever drawn is a fact about the C, not about the colour in it, and Singles’ unused COL_WHITE is exactly the case that would fool a test on colours alone.
singles, range
Undead’s mirrors — not a table at all
The one exception decided by neither the palette nor a slot. Undead’s mirrors and its monsters’ strokes are drawn in the same colour slot, and the mirrors must turn over while the monsters must not. What separates them is the C’s own difference between a stroke and a bar: every draw_line in the game is inside draw_monster and arrives at width 1 exactly, and the mirror is the game’s only draw_thick_line. So the rule is on the line width, in the renderer.
